sources.title: Fossil isotope evidence for trophic simplification on modern Caribbean reefs

currentWindow.coverageNote: The Baltic analysis provides continuous but differently bounded monitoring records for seven sub-basins. The Caribbean reconstruction compares prehistoric reefs with modern deposits whose majority radiocarbon dates span 1926–2014. caribbeanReefTrophicStructure.interpretation: The isotope reconstruction directly establishes substantial simplification in two Caribbean reef regions. These percentages describe trophic structure relative to prehistoric reefs; they are not percentages of the global ocean collapsed.

balticFoodWebStatus.persistenceFinding: Some altered food-web regimes remained after reductions in pressures that contributed to the initial shift.
balticFoodWebStatus.attributionFinding: Multiple pressures were associated with reorganization; warming contributed in several sub-basins and sometimes amplified other pressures.
balticFoodWebStatus.interpretation: The Baltic record establishes long-running regional reorganization and persistence. It does not isolate climate as the sole cause or provide a global affected-distribution denominator.

globalReach.interpretation: Two Caribbean reef regions and seven Baltic sub-basins demonstrate occurrence and regional persistence, but cannot be extrapolated to a global marine-food-web share.

humanConsequences.interpretation: People living near or depending on reefs are exposure and dependence context. The admitted sources do not quantify unique people suffering a terminal health, food, livelihood or essential-service consequence from food-web reorganization.

excludedUses: Do not treat the approximately one billion people near or relying on reefs as people harmed.
Do not treat the 25% of marine species associated with reefs, the number of sub-basins, the number of samples or the length of the records as harm reach.
Do not map a 20–70% trophic-range reduction directly to a 20–70% global movement toward ecosystem collapse.
Do not attribute all Baltic reorganization to climate warming; fishing, nutrient loading, hypoxia, contaminants and other pressures remain active.

coverage.text: Today, 153 countries rely on transboundary waters flowing across or into other countries . Yet according to a new report by UNESCO and UNECE, only 28% of these countries have effective agreements to co-manage most of these vital resources [1] . The report also warns that, if current trends persist, barely one-third of these countries will have effective co-management arrangements in place by 2030.

progress.text: The report notes an improvement in shared water cooperation between 2017 (only 23 countries, or 15%, with most of transboundary basin area covered) and 2023 (43 countries, or 28%). Europe, North America and sub-Saharan Africa show the highest levels of cooperation: 39 out of 84 countries (46%) from these regions have most of their transboundary basin area covered by operational arrangements.

climateReadiness.text: Nearly two-thirds of transboundary river and lake basins include climate adaptation as a task for their joint management bodies. However, today only 14% have adopted a concrete strategy to face this challenge, and just 20% have adopted a joint strategy for disaster risk reduction. facts.operationalEventFrequency: Positive or negative phases occur on average every three to five years.

currentExposureUpdate2023.interpretation: This independently confirms a recent peat-fire smoke episode and widespread exposure. Exposure and pollutant mass do not add to the 2019 death count or enter harmed-person reach.

ecosystemFunction.geography: northern non-permafrost boreal and temperate peatlands
ecosystemFunction.interpretation: The modelled changes establish material loss of peatland carbon-regulation function. A percentage change in carbon uptake is not automatically the same percentage movement toward whole-ecosystem collapse.

postFireRecovery.interpretation: A recent burned peat plateau remained a carbon source for four years, while a 13–15-year-old site returned to a weak sink but retained disturbed soil and vegetation. Twenty years is a source-modelled recovery assumption, not a universal measured recovery time.

mappedCurrentExtent.denominatorDerivation: FAO states that approximately 80% of global peatlands equals around 390 million hectares; 390 / 0.8 gives an approximate 487.5-million-hectare context denominator.
mappedCurrentExtent.interpretation: The approximate one-percent comparison supports a level-2 extent centrally but remains bounded because the numerator and denominator come from different mapping products and the Canadian event is not a complete global fire inventory.

boundary.uniqueHarmedPeople: Use modelled excess deaths for reach. Do not use all residents or people exposed to unhealthy air as harmed people.
boundary.ecosystemExtent: Use mapped burned peatland area against a declared peatland-area denominator. Do not use carbon mass, national land area or all wildfire area as ecosystem reach.
boundary.persistence: Use documented consequence or recovery duration. Do not use publication age, fire-record length, or peat age as persistence.
boundary.overlap: Do not add smoke-exposure, PM2.5, carbon-emission, wildfire-regime, peatland-degradation, permafrost-thaw or global-temperature node scores.

excludedUses: Do not convert the 74.7 million residents of Sumatra and Kalimantan or 1.62 million people exposed in Central Kalimantan into harmed-person reach.
Do not add the 2019 excess-death estimate to a 2023 exposure count or treat repeated events as different severity points.
Do not treat carbon emitted, PM2.5 concentration, sensor count, study years or carbon-stock age as people or ecosystem reach.
Do not equate a 35% change in carbon uptake with 35% movement toward whole-ecosystem collapse.
Do not treat a source-modelled twenty-year carbon-balance period as a universal measured recovery time.
Do not inherit or add scores from PM2.5, Smoke Exposure, Carbon Emission, Wildfire Regime Shift, Peatland Degradation, Permafrost Thaw or Global Temperature.

sources.title: Assessing the success of marine ecosystem restoration using meta-analysis

globalMappedChange.interpretation: Complete mapped loss establishes collapse of the defining habitat at affected pixels. The four-percent share sets global reach against the same mapped seagrass denominator. Dense-to-sparse change is retained separately as degradation and is not added without proving categories are mutually exclusive.

globalRestorationEvidence.interpretation: Restoration is possible but variable. Survival of reintroduced plants is not the same as complete recovery of habitat structure, biodiversity or ecosystem function, so it constrains reversibility without proving full recovery time.

directRecoveryCase.recoveryState: target seagrass recolonization remained incomplete at seven years
directRecoveryCase.interpretation: This source establishes that some physically damaged seagrass meadows remain incompletely recovered after seven years and that succession can take decades. It is a local recovery bound, not a global recovery distribution.

boundary.humanDomain: No compatible current unique-person consequence is attributed specifically to mapped seagrass decline. Fisheries, shoreline protection, water quality and carbon services remain downstream pathways or separate nodes.
boundary.severity: Use complete conversion of an affected seagrass pixel for local severity. Do not use four-percent global loss or map coverage as local severity.
boundary.reach: Use the four-percent complete-loss share against the mapped seagrass distribution. Keep dense-to-sparse degradation separate unless category overlap is resolved.
boundary.persistence: Use documented recovery state and recovery duration. Do not use the map-comparison interval, publication year or restoration-study count as persistence.

excludedUses: Do not infer harmed-person reach from coastal population, fishery dependence, beneficiary counts, country rows or global map coverage.
Do not use the four-percent global loss share as both local severity and ecosystem reach.
Do not add four-percent complete loss and 4.2-percent dense-to-sparse degradation without a verified non-overlapping classification.
Do not treat plant survival as complete ecosystem recovery or intervention failure as ecological irreversibility.
Do not use the four-year map comparison, seven-year monitoring period, 764 interventions or publication age as automatic persistence.
Do not inherit or add scores from Blue Carbon Habitat Loss, Mangrove Buffer Loss, Coastal Habitat Conversion, Fisheries, Carbon Emissions or Sea-Level Rise.
